AskEnvelope.description:
One answer to one question asked in words.

A discriminated envelope rather than one flattened result shape: the routes
return genuinely different things — ranked people, the people one person can
reach, the bridges themselves, two sides weighed against each other — and a
common row would throw away whichever part did not fit.

Read `route` first, then the field it names. Exactly one is populated.

The last two are **two-part** answers, and neither is paginated: a
comparison is a fixed pair and a fan-out a fixed number of drill-downs, so
there is no window to advance. `next_cursor` is null on both, and it means
"there are no pages" rather than "you reached the last one".

Here rather than on a `meta`, because a two-part answer carries one per part and the charge covers the whole question. Priced like a relationship page, or flat like `/relationships/institutions` when it was routed there.

Coverage.description:
How much of the addressable set this answer represents (`W-108`).

The differentiator, stated as data. Every agentic-search product answers "here
are some results"; measured recall across the field runs 19-61% against 77-84%
precision, because an unbounded web has no denominator and nobody can say what
was missed. Ours is countable, so `universe` is a real number and
`enumeration_recall` is a real fraction rather than a claim.

`universe_exhausted` is the one thing a web-scale competitor structurally cannot
return: every matching record was enumerated and the count agrees. It is never
inferred from an agent's confidence -- it requires the enumeration and the count
to match -- and the numbers that justify it ship beside it so a caller can check
the arithmetic instead of trusting the label.

constraints_unmet.description: Requirements in your query that the search could not express, in your own words. Non-empty means part of the question was not answered -- most often because it needs a dataset this search cannot reach (job postings, employment history, patents, news, funding dates). When this is non-empty, `universe_exhausted` is withheld: 'we returned everything that matches' cannot be true of a question that was never asked.
constraints_unmet.title: Constraints Unmet

criteria.description: Per criterion: evaluated, passed, success_rate, and whether it was *proven* by the query or *judged* by a model. Without this a thin result leaves the caller guessing which requirement thinned it.

Non-empty therefore means `universe_exhausted` is withheld by construction: we returned everything reachable, and a dataset cannot see the rest.

EntityCategory.description:
*What* to search, and what a returned row is.

One parameter carries both, because they are the same fact: a search of
`patent` returns patents. The alternative — a `source`/`vertical` selector
beside a narrower `category` — lets a caller ask for patents from the
people index, a combination that has no meaning and would need rejecting
at runtime. A closed set that cannot express the contradiction is better
than a validator that catches it.

Values are exactly prism's own row types, so `category` in the request and
`results[].category` in the response are always the same string.

`company` and `person` are the GTM index; the rest are separate corpora
with their own filters, freshness and coverage. Not everything applies
everywhere: see `SearchRequest`, which rejects the GTM-only parameters
rather than ignoring them.

`job_opening` is a document corpus like `patent`/`news_article`/etc — a
posting, not an entity — but its records carry a domain (the posting
company's) all the same. It is deliberately **not** in `GTM_CATEGORIES`
(that set is about the entity/document distinction, and a job posting is
still a document), but it *is* in `DOMAIN_FILTERABLE_CATEGORIES`, which
exists specifically to separate those two axes.

lists the accepted names and an OpenAPI enum callers can read, and neither
of those is something a hand-written check gives you.

NamedDocumentEntitiesRequest.description:
`POST /v1/entities/{news,market-reports,fundings,job-openings}`
(DEC-052, DEC-053).

from their internal id (see the other three: a patent number, a trend
name and a DOI already *are* the id, so they keep the plain
`DocumentEntitiesRequest` above with no `by` at all).

real hit on several funding rounds, and a job title like `"Software

simply the mode where it can hold more than one entry, while `by="id"`
always resolves to exactly one. Job-openings' `matches` are ordered
most-recent-first rather than by match score, the one place this
category's `by="name"` diverges from the others.

PeopleConstraints.description:
Which people on one side of a relationship count.

These hang off a company rather than off the request, because a
relationship has two sides and they are constrained independently.
"Directors at Acme who know anyone at Globex" and "anyone at Acme who knows
directors at Globex" are different questions, and a request-level seniority
filter cannot tell them apart — it would constrain both at once.

Only three axes, because the affiliation corpus carries only three. It holds
no firmographics, so industry, headcount, funding and technology cannot be
applied to the people on a relationship at all. They are rejected rather
than ignored: `POST /v1/search` is where those questions belong.

department.description: Department (Function) labels, the same vocabulary the org chart uses: one of the 23 Function names, or the `General` / `Others` sentinels. Renamed as of 2026-08 — e.g. `Engineering / Software` (was `Engineering & Technical`), `IT & Infrastructure` (was `Information Technology`), `Human Resources / People`, `Medical & Health`, `Legal, Risk & Compliance`. `Data, Analytics & AI` and `Security` are now their own Functions rather than children of engineering and IT.

seniority.description: Seniority levels. Exactly 7 values, most senior first: `C-Suite`, `VP`, `Director / Head`, `Manager`, `IC`, `Entry`, `In Training`. Note `Director` and `Head` are ONE level, spelled `Director / Head`. The pre-2026-08 vocabulary (`C Suite` without the hyphen, `Director`, `Head`, `Senior`, `President`, `Intern`, `Founder`, `Owner`, `Partner`, `Investor`, `Advisor`, `Consultant`, `Freelancer`, `Educator`, `Healthcare Professional`, `Utility Worker`, `Speciality Service Provider`, `Unemployed`) is no longer indexed and matches nothing. Founder / Owner / Partner / Investor / Advisor are governance roles and Consultant / Freelancer are employment types; neither is filterable on this axis, and the remaining four are departments, not levels.

RelationKind.description:
Which relationship question `POST /v1/relationships` is answering.

Closed set — it appears in `resolved_search.filters.relation`.

Named for the *question*, not for the upstream's internal query shapes.
Prism has its own vocabulary for how a relationship is executed, several
members of which are the same question asked from a different angle; a
public enum that tracks an internal one becomes a breaking change the first
time the internal one is refactored. The mapping lives in
`app/retrieval/prism.py` and is this contract's business, not the caller's.

Both are *bridge* questions: people at one company who share an
institution — a former employer, or a school — with the other side. None of
them answers "one person who worked at both A and B". That question is not
expressible on the affiliation corpus at all, because the field naming a
person's employer holds their single current one, denormalized onto every
edge; a query written against it matches nobody and reads as "no such
people". Asking for it is a 422, not an empty page.
RelationKind.title: RelationKind

RelationshipAskRequest.description:
`POST /v1/relationships/ask` — a relationship question in words.

Deliberately three fields. This is the sentences-only surface: every
structural knob lives on the three typed routes, and adding them here would
recreate the thing it exists to remove — a caller having to know which
endpoint answers their question before they can ask it.

A new route rather than a widened `POST /v1/relationships`, for three reasons
that each stand alone. The cursor fingerprint is a hash over the whole
serialised body, so **any** field added to that request invalidates every
cursor in flight. The three routes return genuinely different shapes, and
that route's typed response model is a contract worth keeping. And a new
route carries its own billing action from the first day rather than having a
price split retrofitted onto a flat one.

cursor.description: Page on. The cursor carries the plan that was worked out for your question, so paging never re-reads the sentence and never charges for interpreting it twice.
cursor.title: Cursor

query.description:
The question, in words. Any kind of relationship question:

- *who at Adyen do we know from Stripe* — people who bridge two companies
- *is there anyone at Canva who used to work with Melanie Perkins* — who one named person can reach
- *what do Stripe and Adyen people have in common* — the shared employers and schools themselves

Which of the three it turns out to be is worked out for you and reported back as `route`. A question this corpus cannot answer is refused with the reason and, where there is one, the endpoint that does answer it — never answered narrowly.
query.title: Query

RelationshipInstitutionsRequest.description:
`POST /v1/relationships/institutions`.

The institution list on its own — which employers and schools two companies
have people at in common, and how many on each side. `POST /v1/relationships`
already returns this as `institutions[]`, but only alongside a ranked page of
people, which is the expensive half of that answer and often not the half
that was wanted. There was also no way to *narrow* the list without paying
for the ranking again.

No `relation` field: there is only one shape here. A bridge needs two
populations to compare, so `via_institution` — one company plus a named
institution — has no institution list to compute; it is already the answer to
a question that names its own institutions.

No `query` field, and no `cursor`. The upstream route is structured only, and
the answer is a single aggregation rather than a ranked window: `limit` is how
many institutions come back, `truncated` on the response says more exist, and
there is no page 2 to ask for.

companies.description:
Exactly two. A shared institution is a comparison between two populations, so one company has nothing to share and a third has no defined pairing.

**Order still matters**, even though nothing about the returned list looks one-sided. The upstream excludes the **first** company's own institution keys from the bridges and keeps the second's, on purpose: the first company is essentially everyone's current employer on that side, so it bridges nothing, while "previously worked at the *other* company" is the single strongest connection in the corpus and was measured as the top bridge for the highest-ranked row. So swapping the two changes which institutions come back and what `people_first` / `people_second` count. It is not a symmetric request.

Each company's own `people` constraints apply to that side only, and they change both *which* institutions qualify — an institution needs `min_people_per_side` matching people on each side to survive — and the per-side counts returned for the ones that do.
companies.title: Companies

institution_type.description: Restrict the bridges to shared employers, or to schools. Unset returns both, which is the usual question.
institution_type.title: Institution Type

limit.description: How many institutions to return, strongest bridge first. Not a page size — there is no cursor and no page 2. When more exist than this, `truncated` on the response is `true`; raise `limit` or narrow with the filters above to see them.
limit.title: Limit

min_people_per_side.description:
How many distinct people each side must have at an institution for it to count. The quality knob: at the default `1` a single coincidence — one person on each side who happened to attend the same school — is a bridge, and on a large pair of companies those dominate the tail by count.

One consequence worth knowing, because it is not what the name suggests: the threshold is applied to the exact per-side counts *after* the upstream has already trimmed to the strongest `limit` institutions, not before. So a high threshold can return fewer than `limit` institutions while institutions that would have passed it exist further down the untrimmed list. Raise `limit` alongside it when the answer looks short.
min_people_per_side.title: Min People Per Side

name_starts_with.description:
Keep only institutions whose display name **starts with** this, case-insensitively.

A prefix, not a substring and not a fuzzy match: `"stan"` finds Stanford University, and `"ford"` does not. That is the honest limit rather than a simplification — the institution name is a bare keyword in the affiliation corpus with no analysed subfield, so a substring search is not on offer.

It narrows the documents before they are bucketed, so it also makes the answer arrive faster rather than costing anything. For one institution you can already name, send it to `POST /v1/relationships` as an `institutions[]` anchor instead; this is for narrowing a list you have not seen yet.
name_starts_with.title: Name Starts With

paths-to-Acme are different questions against different corpora with
different costs, and `category` could not carry the difference: these rows

SearchMode.description:
How hard to work on the query.

The distinction is *what the words mean*, not how many results come back:

- ``fast``  — match my words. The query is matched by meaning (vector
  retrieval, falling back to keywords where vectors are unavailable); no
  LLM in the path, so nothing is extracted into filters.
- ``auto``  — understand my intent. The parser extracts filters.
- ``deep``  — reason about it. Multi-step, slowest, most expensive.

`fast` was very nearly defined as "filters only, no LLM", which would have
made `query` — the primary parameter — silently inert. A parameter that
does nothing is worse than one that is missing.
SearchMode.title: SearchMode

category.description: What to search. Omit it to have prism classify `query` and pick a category automatically (`POST /v1/search/query` upstream). Each keyword is a phrase (words up to 2 apart), singular or plural, matched in the company's name, keyword tags, products and descriptions. Results are ordered by how much of what the company says about itself is about the keywords. `company` only; combines with `filters`, domains and `sort`, never with `query`. No AI reading runs, so `fast` and `auto` run it identically, at the Basic rate; `deep` is refused. Echoed back as `resolved_search.keyword_query`.

SearchSuggestion.description:
A better way to have asked this question.

Advisory only. The search the caller asked for is the search that ran and
the search these `results` came from — this says a *different* request
would probably have answered better.

The split is **search vs agentic**, because that is the bigger question
and the one a caller answers first:

- `kind: "search"` — a plain `POST /v1/search` still answers this, just
  not in the category it was asked in. `category` names the one that
  fits, and drops straight into the next request.
- `kind: "agentic"` — no single search answers this, whatever the
  category: it needs several steps, or several corpora joined. `category`
  is null, because the category is not the problem. Act on it with
  `POST /v1/agents`.

There is deliberately **no `mode` field**. `mode: deep` does run the
agentic engine, so naming it here was tempting and wrong: the customer-
facing agentic surface is its own endpoint, and a suggestion that said
`deep` would point at a parameter rather than at the thing that actually
answers the question.

Never the category the caller already searched: "you should have searched
what you searched" is noise, and it is suppressed upstream rather than
left for a client to filter. Null on the common case, on every page after
the first, and whenever the request carried filters but no `query` —
there is no question to re-place if nobody asked one in words.

kind.description: `search` — a different `category` fits. `agentic` — no single search fits; use `POST /v1/agents`.

SharedInstitutionsEnvelope.description:
`Envelope[SharedInstitution]` — the bridges as the results themselves.

The house list shape rather than a bespoke one: the institutions arrive in
`results`, so a client that already renders an envelope renders this with no
new code path, and `resolved_search` / `attribution` / `degradation` / `meta`
mean here exactly what they mean everywhere else.

**This endpoint is not paginated, so `has_more` is always `False` and
`next_cursor` is always `null`.** That is not "you reached the end of the
pages" — there are no pages. The answer is one aggregation over the
affiliation graph, `limit` is how much of it comes back, and `truncated`
below is how "more qualified than you asked for" is communicated. The two
envelope fields stay present and stay honest about themselves rather than
being dropped: `Envelope`'s invariant is `has_more == (next_cursor is not
None)`, both readings hold at `False`/`null`, and a client that branches on
`has_more` to decide whether to page again correctly decides not to.

columns.description: The answer table's columns, in order, when a run carries extra columns beyond the entity's own fields -- a job-opening link, a value joined from another dataset. Each entry is `{name, description, source}`; the value for each sits on every row in `results` keyed by the column `name`. Null means a plain entity table. Additive, so it breaks no existing client.
columns.title: Columns

coverage.description: How much of the addressable set this answer represents. Null means coverage was not measured for this request -- `fast` and `auto` do not enumerate -- and never that coverage was zero. Additive, so it breaks no existing client.

next_cursor.description: Opaque and signed. Invariant: has_more == (next_cursor is not None). There is no page or offset parameter — not accepted, not deprecated, never present.
next_cursor.title: Next Cursor

suggestion.description: A better way to have asked this question -- a different `category` (`kind: search`), or agentic search via `POST /v1/agents` (`kind: agentic`). Advisory: these `results` came from the search that was asked for, whatever this says. Null when there is nothing worth suggesting, which is the common case. Additive, so it breaks no existing client.

total_is_estimate.description: Always serialized, never defaulted away. A field clients can forget exists is a field that renders an estimate as exact.
total_is_estimate.title: Total Is Estimate

truncated.description:
`true` when more institutions qualified than `limit` returned.

A first-class field rather than a `degradation[]` entry, because it is the one thing about this response a caller must branch on and `has_more` — the field they would normally read for it — is structurally `false` here. A clipped list that looked complete would be a wrong answer rather than a short one: `institutions` is frequently the whole point ("you both know people from Stanford and McKinsey").

Raise `limit`, or narrow with `institution_type` / `name_starts_with`, to see the rest. `degradation[]` still carries anything the upstream itself reported about the answer being narrower than the question; this field is not restated there, because one condition reported twice is a condition clients learn to ignore.
truncated.title: Truncated

for would be indefensible -- so this route is named in the billing test's
free-under-a-metered-prefix list rather than inferred.

get.description:
What this tenant can spend on the data platform.

All three numbers are real now that grants carry a `platform_code`
(`SDP-15`):

- `allocated` — credits earmarked to dsp specifically.
- `shared` — the tenant's unrestricted credits. **Reported but not
  spendable here**: dsp is hard-capped (`SDP-30`), so an exhausted
  allocation is a 402 rather than a quiet fall-through onto the Account OS
  balance. It is reported anyway because an empty allocation beside a
  healthy shared balance must read as "move some across", not as an empty
  account.
- `spendable` — the headline, and the one that agrees with what a charge
  will actually allow.

`scope` says which of those two worlds produced the answer, so a caller can
tell a real per-platform figure from the legacy tenant-wide fallback that
an un-upgraded mint still returns.

get.description:
What this credential has reported, newest first.

Scoped by construction, not by a filter the caller passes: the tenant comes
from the session and the actor from the credential, so a person who belongs
to two organisations sees each one's reports only while signed into it, and
never a colleague's.

`total` counts what the caller has, under that same visibility, so a pager
can tell a full page from the last one without asking for the next — and it
narrows with the filters, or a pager would offer pages nothing can fill.

A filter value we do not recognise is a `422` rather than an empty list. An
empty list here reads as "you never reported that", which is a different
fact from "that is not a tag", and a typo would otherwise look like good
news.

Spend for the calling key.

Only the calling key: reading another key's usage needs a scope that does
not exist, and inventing one before the dashboard exists would be guessing
at who may see whose spend.

**Key-authenticated only** (`SDP-27`). mint answers `400 not_a_key_principal`
for a human token, and our client translates any non-200 into
`CreditsUnavailable` → 503 — telling the dashboard that mint is down when
the question was simply malformed. Same misdirection class as the signup
404-mapped-to-503 already recorded in `09`, so the refusal happens here.

The consequence is honest and worth stating: the dashboard cannot show
usage at all, because it has no key to call with. That needs a
tenant-scoped usage endpoint in mint (`W-66`).

post.description:
Is this person one of ours, and may they act here?

Exists because `GET /v1/members` cannot answer it for a key. That route
forwards the caller's own token to auth-service, and a key's delegation
token carries no user at all — so an integration that must attribute work
to a person before spending the organisation's credits had no way to ask.
dsp-slack is the first: Slack is a shared prompt, and a run nobody can be
billed for is the failure it exists to prevent.

One email per call, not a listing. A key asking "is this specific person a
member" needs one bit; handing it the roster would disclose every
colleague's address to an integration that never needed them.

post.summary: Resolve one email to a member of the credential's organisation

post.description:
How one company's people distribute across departments and seniorities.

**This is a matrix, not a tree.** The corpus holds no reporting lines — no
person document carries a manager — so there is no hierarchy here to walk.
What you get is every person we hold for the company, grouped by two closed
vocabularies: the department taxonomy down the rows and the seniority ladder
across the columns. Both carry an explicit **Unknown** entry, always last,
for the people we could not place on that axis.

How people are counted:

* **Each person once, at their most senior level.** `total` is the number of
  people, and it equals the sum of the seniority columns.
* **In every department they hold.** A department row's total is the sum of
  its cells, so the rows (and the cells) can add up to more than `total`.
* **Suspect profiles are left out** unless `include_suspects` is true;
  `suspect_count` says how many.

Every taxonomy value is `{code, label}`: send the `code` back as a filter
value, show the `label`. `subdepartments` breaks each row one level finer,
with its own seniority counts. `metrics` asks for the per-cell badges —
`new_joiners` (joined in the last 180 days) and `job_openings` (open
roles) — and `metrics` in the response says how each one went.

Narrow with `filters` and the counts change rather than the display: a
country filter returns that country's org chart, not the global one with
cells hidden. `POST /v1/org-chart/locations` lists the places. `state` is
`ready`, `empty` (`no_profiles`) or `degraded` (`low_coverage`: the record
is sparsely profiled, and `coverage` says how and lists the other records
of the same company).

post.description:
Who is connected to whom, over which shared employers and schools.

Two questions, chosen with `relation`:

- **`between_companies`** — people at the **first** company who are
  connected to people at the second. Order is the contract: swap them and
  you get the mirror question.
- **`via_institution`** — people at one company affiliated with named
  institutions.

Every row carries `via`: which institutions connect them, and how confident
each match is. That is the answer, not decoration — a person with no reason
is not a connection.

Two limits worth knowing before you build on this. A connection here means a
**shared institution**, not a personal acquaintance: two people who both
worked at Palantir may never have met. And this cannot answer "one person
who worked at both A and B" — that is a different question the corpus cannot
express, and asking for it is a 422 rather than an empty page.

To expand one row into the people they can actually reach, and how they know
each other, send its `id` to `POST /v1/relationships/reach`.

post.summary: Ask a relationship question in words

post.description:
Which employers and schools two companies both have people at.

The bridges on their own, as `results`, with how many distinct people each
company has at each one. `POST /v1/relationships` returns the same list as a
side-field, but only alongside a ranked page of people — and that ranking is
the expensive half of the work, plus a hydration lookup per row. This route
runs the bridge aggregation and stops there, so it is the cheap way to ask
"what do these two actually have in common" and the only way to *filter* that
list without paying for the people again.

**Order matters, even here.** The first company's own institution keys are
excluded from the bridges and the second company's are kept, deliberately:
essentially everyone on the first side has that company as their current
employer, so it bridges nobody, while having previously worked at the
*second* company is the strongest connection the corpus holds. Swap the two
and you get a different list with different counts.

Four ways to narrow it, each of which changes which institutions qualify
rather than just what is displayed:

- `companies[].people` — department, seniority and country, applied to that
  side alone. An institution has to keep enough matching people on **both**
  sides to survive, so filtering one side can remove bridges entirely.
- `institution_type` — shared employers only, or schools only.
- `min_people_per_side` — drops one-person coincidences. Applied after the
  upstream trim to `limit`, so a high threshold can return fewer than `limit`
  institutions even when more would have passed it.
- `name_starts_with` — a case-insensitive **prefix** on the display name, not
  a substring: `"stan"` finds Stanford, `"ford"` does not.

Each row's `id` is the affiliation corpus's own key, and it round-trips: send
it back to `POST /v1/relationships` as an `institutions[]` anchor (`by` is
detected as `inst_key`) to get the people who are connected through that one
institution.

Two things to expect rather than be surprised by. Only the exact key forms
the upstream resolved for the first company are excluded, so a company's own
institution can still appear under an alternate key form — `name:microsoft`
beside `linkedin.com/company/microsoft` — carrying its own employees'
count. And this route is **not paginated**: `has_more` is always `false` and
`next_cursor` always `null`, `limit` is the whole list, and `truncated` says
whether more qualified.

Priced flat per call, whatever comes back: one aggregation is the same work
whether it finds three bridges or two hundred.

post.description:
Expand one person into the people they can reach at a company.

The drill-down of `POST /v1/relationships`, and callable on its own: send a
`person.li_url` — which that route returns on every row as `linkedin_url` —
and you never have to run the list query first.

Every row says *how*: the shared institution, both people's roles and dates
there, and how many months they overlap. By default only overlapping tenure
counts, because a shared former employer without it means very little on a
large company — everyone who ever worked there shares it. Set
`connection_basis` to `shared` for the broader reading; it is echoed back,
because it decides which rows exist at all.

`institutions` summarises the same answer the rows spell out one person at a
time: every institution the two sides connect through, and how many people
at the target each one reaches. It describes the whole answer rather than
this page, so it is often the readable version — "everyone you reach here,
you reach through Microsoft" — and it is what you send back to
`POST /v1/relationships` as an `institutions[]` anchor to narrow.

Priced the same as `POST /v1/relationships`: it reads the same corpus and
costs the same upstream work.

get.description:
The values one filter accepts — for autocomplete and pickers.

**Geography is the one place the name here differs from the name you
filter by.** `geo` spans four levels and has no single vocabulary, so it
is not a name this route accepts. Enumerate places one level at a time
(`country`, `state`, `city`, `region`) and feed the answer back as
`geo.places[].value` with that same `level`.

**Two-level filters.** `industry` and `department` are parent/child. Ask for
the rows with `level=parents`, then one branch at a time with
`parent=<name>` as the user expands it. `department` cannot be done any
other way: its plain value list is all 248 values of both levels with
nothing marking which is which. `level=children` gives the other rung,
de-duplicated.
